sections.html:
Winona is a small river city on the Mississippi with a large student population and a lot of rental property. Houses here cost far less than in the Twin Cities suburbs, and the local rules that matter most cover rentals, permits and short-term stays.

Your choices are an agent listing, a private sale, or a cash offer straight from a buyer. The right one turns on how the house is holding up and how quickly you have to be done.

Rentals are the main thing to sort out. With so many student and investor rentals in town, buyers ask early about the license, the date of the last inspection and the tenants' plans. Put the answers on paper and the negotiation moves faster on any route. If the house has always been owner-occupied, the main items are open permits, the basement and the furnace.

The population estimate for July 1, 2025 is 26,530, up 2.1% from 25,997 in April 2020. The city lost people between 2010 and 2020, so the recent gain is a reversal. Figures for 2020 to 2024:

  • 10,786 households averaging 2.13 people
  • 58.0% of homes owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied value: $201,800
  • Median gross rent: $882
  • Median household income: $56,337

Sellers tend to be older owners downsizing or heirs settling a parent's house. Buyers are often first-timers or investors. Condition and location set your real price, so ask for a written offer or an agent's estimate first.

Winona was laid out in 1852 and 1853, and much of its housing is old. Two historic districts on the National Register of Historic Places combine into one local historic district under the city's Heritage Preservation Commission. If your house is in that district, ask the city's planning office what review applies before you promise a buyer changes to the exterior.

Winona is bluff country, hilly, with the river on one side and Lock and Dam 5A across it. Houses face hot humid summers and cold snowy winters. Buyers commonly ask about basements, furnaces and roofs, and about whether a property near the river sits in a mapped floodplain. Ask the city's inspections office or your insurer to confirm the status of your address, and mention any past water in the basement in your written disclosure.

Any rental unit in the city must hold a license before tenants move in, and Chapter 33A of the housing code requires an inspection every five years. When the house you are selling is a rental, expect the buyer to check the license and inspection history.

The licensing steps are short:

  1. Planning and Zoning confirms that the property may be a rental.
  2. The owner submits a rental license application.
  3. The Building Inspections Department inspects the unit.
  4. The fee is paid, due upfront for a new rental.
  5. The property must meet the housing code before the license is issued.

The city also provides a Rental License Transfer of Ownership application, which a buyer of a rental house will need. Call Planning and Zoning at 507-457-8250 to ask whether your property qualifies as a rental, and the inspections office at 507-457-8231 to schedule.

Certification carries an inspection fee once every five years. City Code Chapter 51 sets the amounts, and the current schedule began January 1, 2026.

Winona rental housing inspection fees
Property typeCalculationTotal
Single-family dwelling$100 per unit plus $100 per building$200
Duplex$200 for two units plus $100 per building$300
Owner-occupied duplex$100 for one unit plus $100 per building$200
Sleeping room$45 per room plus $100 per building$145 for one room

In an owner-occupied duplex, the unit the owner lives in isn't certified, so only one unit is charged.

A buyer can use a Winona house as a short-term rental only with a license and a public hearing. The city calls these Tourist Homes and defines them as buildings that provide sleeping accommodations to transient guests for up to 29 consecutive days. There are two classes, owner-occupied and non-owner-occupied, each with its own regulations.

  • Every short-term rental needs an inspection and a license.
  • Residential zoning districts require a Planning Commission public hearing before licensing.
  • A 4% hotel and motel tax on monthly rent has applied since July 1, 2018.

If your house has hosted Airbnb-style stays, gather the license paperwork for the buyer. If it hasn't, assume a new owner can't start without the hearing.

A building permit is required for additions, alterations, new construction, remodeling and most replacements. Work that needs none includes painting, cabinets, countertops, floor coverings, tiling, storage sheds under 200 square feet, retaining walls up to 4 feet and decks not over 30 inches above grade, unless attached to a permanent structure.

Fences usually need no permit, but ask Planning and Zoning at 507-457-8250 first. Fences may reach 6 feet in the rear and 4 feet on the street side, and anything over 7 feet needs a variance and a permit. The city doesn't issue electrical permits, so electrical questions go to the state electrical inspector. An unpermitted deck or finished basement is something a buyer's inspector will notice, so close out any open permits before you list.

The county auditor receives a certificate of real estate value for any sale above $3,000, and Minnesota Statutes 272.115 bars homestead status for the buyer if it is missing. The assessor drops the homestead classification after a sale until the new owner applies and qualifies.

The house sits in Winona County, so the deed is recorded with the county recorder there. Ask the county for current recording fees and the deed tax calculation, and have your title company confirm who files the certificate. Minnesota also lets a seller pass the required disclosure to the buyer's agent instead of the buyer directly.

Gather the rental license, permit closeouts and repair receipts before you accept an offer. A cash sale skips the lender and appraisal, so the schedule follows the county paperwork and any rental or permit items, and the buyer takes the house in its current state. With a listing, add showings and the buyer's loan on top. Either way, bring photo ID for every owner who signs and keep copies of the paperwork you gathered, so the title company can close without chasing you for documents.

faqs.q: Does Winona require an inspection before I sell my house?
faqs.a: Winona's inspection program covers rental units, which need a license renewed through an inspection every five years. For a house you live in, ask the inspections office at 507-457-8231 whether anything applies to your address.

faqs.q: How much is a rental inspection in Winona?
faqs.a: A single-family rental costs $200 total, made of $100 per unit and $100 per building, under the schedule effective January 1, 2026. A duplex is $300.

faqs.q: Can I sell a rental house to a new owner in Winona?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer files a Rental License Transfer of Ownership application, and the property must still meet the housing code. Planning and Zoning at 507-457-8250 can confirm that the property is eligible.

faqs.q: Are Airbnb stays allowed in Winona?
faqs.a: They are allowed with a license. The city treats them as Tourist Homes for stays up to 29 days, requires an inspection and a hearing in residential districts, and charges a 4% hotel and motel tax.

faqs.q: What is the typical home value in Winona?
faqs.a: The median owner-occupied value is $201,800 for 2020 to 2024. Your own number depends on condition and location, so get a written offer or a local agent's estimate before you decide.
